title: Nowcasting and Ensemble Forecasting of Seasonal Respiratory Hospitalisations
content:
Surveillance data on influenza-like illness, laboratory confirmations and syndromic emergency visits differ in latency, completeness and bias, which complicates real-time modelling. The study was funded through an institutional grant, and the funder had no role in the design of the methods or the interpretation of the results. Our collaborators at the fictional Northvale Institute of Public Health requested forecasts at horizons of one to four weeks for regional planning. The model and data choices made in this study reflect a balance between realism and tractability, and each choice is justified in the sections that follow. Ensemble forecasts that combine several epidemic models have repeatedly outperformed individual models in the weekly forecast hubs run during respiratory virus seasons. We evaluated forecasts of weekly incident hospitalisations for a seasonal respiratory pathogen over a multi-season period in a mid-sized national health system. The motivating problem was that reporting delays caused early nowcasts of incident infections to be revised sharply as late-arriving records were added.

Model parameters were estimated by standard fitting routines, and convergence diagnostics were examined for every model that entered the results. Forecasts were scored using the weighted interval score and the empirical coverage of nominal fifty and ninety percent prediction intervals. The nowcasting model treated the delay between symptom onset and report as a discrete distribution estimated from historical line lists, with a day-of-week effect on reporting. Rt was estimated with a renewal equation that links incident infections to past infections through a generation interval distribution, with a smoothness prior on log Rt. Each forecast was produced in real time using only the data version available on the forecast date, so that later reporting revisions could not leak into the evaluation. A held-out portion of the data was reserved for validation and was not used for any tuning decision in the study. Observation noise was modelled with a negative binomial distribution to account for overdispersion in weekly counts of hospital admissions.

The ensemble forecast achieved a lower weighted interval score than every component model at horizons of two to four weeks. Nowcasts of incident infections for the most recent three days were revised by a median of eighteen percent once complete reports arrived. The renewal model performed best during stable periods, whereas the time-series model was more competitive near the seasonal peak. The results were stable across the sensitivity analyses described in the methods, with only small changes in the central estimates. Including mobility covariates improved forecasts only modestly and mainly in the regions where mobility changed abruptly. Forecasts of hospital admissions were more accurate than forecasts of laboratory-confirmed cases, which depended heavily on testing policy. The results are presented first in aggregate and then broken down by the main strata of the study.

The generation interval distribution is itself uncertain, and shifting its mean by one day changed estimates of Rt by several percent. Structural disagreement between the component models was a large part of the ensemble spread near turning points of the epidemic. Uncertainty in the results arises from several sources, including the data, the model structure, and the choices made during analysis. A limitation of the study is that some sources of uncertainty could not be quantified and are therefore described only qualitatively. Prediction intervals widened appropriately with horizon, but the models were overconfident when a new variant altered transmissibility. Past forecast errors suggest that intervention effects, such as school closures, are the dominant source of unforecastable change in incidence.

Operational nowcasting and ensemble forecasting can support planning, provided that forecasts are issued with honest intervals and evaluated prospectively. The experience from this season shows the value of retrospective evaluation against the final, fully reported data. The supplementary material contains the full tables, the model specification, and a description of the data used in the study. Future work should integrate wastewater surveillance and serological data to anchor estimates of true infection incidence. The forecast hub model, in which several teams submit standardised quantile forecasts, offers a transparent way to compare epidemic models over time. Taken together, the results suggest that the approach is useful, although further study with additional data would strengthen the conclusions.

title: Estimating Rt in Real Time: Forecast Evaluation Across Epidemic Waves
content:
We report the study motivation, the data sources, the model specification, and the main results in a single account intended for practitioners and researchers alike. The effective reproduction number Rt summarises how many secondary infections each case generates at a given time, and its trajectory signals whether an epidemic is growing or declining. The motivating problem was that reporting delays caused early nowcasts of incident infections to be revised sharply as late-arriving records were added. The model and data choices made in this study reflect a balance between realism and tractability, and each choice is justified in the sections that follow. Surveillance data on influenza-like illness, laboratory confirmations and syndromic emergency visits differ in latency, completeness and bias, which complicates real-time modelling. We evaluated forecasts of weekly incident hospitalisations for a seasonal respiratory pathogen over a multi-season period in a mid-sized national health system. Our collaborators at the fictional Northvale Institute of Public Health requested forecasts at horizons of one to four weeks for regional planning.

Rt was estimated with a renewal equation that links incident infections to past infections through a generation interval distribution, with a smoothness prior on log Rt. Mobility indicators and vaccination coverage were included as covariates in some models to represent changes in contact patterns and population susceptibility. Model parameters were estimated by standard fitting routines, and convergence diagnostics were examined for every model that entered the results. Ensemble forecasts were built as weighted quantile averages, with weights set by the recent weighted interval score of each component model. The study protocol was written before the analysis began, and departures from it are listed explicitly in the supplementary material. The nowcasting model treated the delay between symptom onset and report as a discrete distribution estimated from historical line lists, with a day-of-week effect on reporting. Forecasts were scored using the weighted interval score and the empirical coverage of nominal fifty and ninety percent prediction intervals.

Forecast skill declined as the horizon lengthened, and the advantage of the ensemble over the baseline was largest at the three-week horizon. Estimates of Rt tracked the turning points of each seasonal wave with a lag of roughly five days relative to the final retrospective estimates. Where the data were sparse, the results are reported with explicit caution and should be read as indicative rather than conclusive. The renewal model performed best during stable periods, whereas the time-series model was more competitive near the seasonal peak. Coverage of the ninety percent prediction intervals was close to nominal at short horizons but fell below nominal during the rapid growth phase of the epidemic. The results are presented first in aggregate and then broken down by the main strata of the study. Nowcasts of incident infections for the most recent three days were revised by a median of eighteen percent once complete reports arrived.

Communicating forecast uncertainty to decision makers is as important as estimating it. Whether the forecast concerns next week's hospital admissions or the climate of the coming decades, users tend to read a single central line as a promise, and they discount ranges that are presented without context. We found that fan charts with explicitly labelled probability bands, a plain-language statement of what the forecast does not include, and a short note on past forecast error helped planners to act on probabilistic forecasts. Verbal expressions of likelihood should be mapped to numerical probabilities and used consistently. Forecast uncertainty should be framed as the range of outcomes planners must prepare for, and decision makers should be shown how their choices would change across that range. Forecasters across disciplines can learn from each other on how to present predictive distributions, scenario ranges and calibration without overwhelming the audience.

The experience from this season shows the value of retrospective evaluation against the final, fully reported data. The forecast hub model, in which several teams submit standardised quantile forecasts, offers a transparent way to compare epidemic models over time. Future work should integrate wastewater surveillance and serological data to anchor estimates of true infection incidence. Operational nowcasting and ensemble forecasting can support planning, provided that forecasts are issued with honest intervals and evaluated prospectively. The authors thank the staff of the participating institutions and the anonymous reviewers whose comments improved the study. The supplementary material contains the full tables, the model specification, and a description of the data used in the study.

title: Regional Precipitation Projections from CMIP6 Ensembles After Downscaling
content:
We report the study motivation, the data sources, the model specification, and the main results in a single account intended for practitioners and researchers alike. Downscaling techniques translate coarse global model output into regional detail, using either dynamical regional climate models or statistical relationships learned from observations. We examined projected changes in seasonal precipitation and extreme temperature over a fictional river basin studied by the Halden Climate Research Centre. Systematic biases in simulated temperature and precipitation mean that raw model output cannot be used directly in impact models without correction. The aim of this report is to quantify how much of the spread in regional projections survives after downscaling and bias correction. Climate projection uncertainty has three classic sources: internal variability, model response uncertainty and scenario uncertainty about future emissions. The model and data choices made in this study reflect a balance between realism and tractability, and each choice is justified in the sections that follow.

Models were weighted by a combination of historical skill and inter-model independence, because several CMIP models share code and components. Statistical downscaling relied on a regression approach with large-scale predictors, while dynamical downscaling used a regional climate model driven by a subset of global models. Internal variability was estimated from multiple initial-condition realisations available for a small number of models in the ensemble. We assembled thirty-two CMIP6 models under three shared socioeconomic pathways and extracted monthly temperature and precipitation over the study domain. The methods section describes the data preparation, the model fitting procedure, and the validation design in the order in which they were carried out. Evaluation used a cross-validation design in which bias correction was fitted in one period of the observations and tested in another. All data were screened for completeness and obvious errors before modelling, and records that failed these checks were set aside and counted.

Projected increases in extreme daily precipitation were robust in sign across models, although their magnitude varied by a factor of two. Weighting the ensemble by skill narrowed the projected range slightly but did not shift the median change by a large amount. The results are presented first in aggregate and then broken down by the main strata of the study. The ensemble median projected a substantial rise in mean winter temperature, with the inter-model range exceeding the median change for precipitation in several months. Quantile mapping altered the projected trend in some models, which raises the question of whether the correction preserves the climate change signal. Downscaling added meaningful spatial detail in mountainous parts of the basin, where the global models placed the wrong elevation and rain shadow. Where the data were sparse, the results are reported with explicit caution and should be read as indicative rather than conclusive.

A limitation of the study is that some sources of uncertainty could not be quantified and are therefore described only qualitatively. Bias correction assumes that model biases remain stationary under a changed climate, an assumption that may fail for processes such as snow cover feedback. Climate projection uncertainty cannot be reduced to a single number, because it combines internal variability, structural model differences and emissions scenarios. Our decomposition shows that the share of variance attributable to model response grows with lead time and with spatial detail. The uncertainty estimates themselves rest on assumptions, and we discuss the extent to which those assumptions may fail. Probabilistic statements derived from the ensemble should be described as conditional on the scenario and on the choice of models and weighting.

Taken together, the results suggest that the approach is useful, although further study with additional data would strengthen the conclusions. Future ensembles should be designed to sample structural uncertainty more systematically and should document model dependence. Users of regional projections should be given the full range of plausible outcomes and not only the ensemble mean. We recommend reporting both raw and bias-corrected projections so that users can judge how much the correction contributes to the stated results. The main limitations of the study concern the data, the model assumptions, and the generalisability of the results to other settings. Emerging machine learning downscaling methods deserve evaluation against the same cross-validated benchmarks as the traditional approaches.

title: Workflow Capture and Provenance for Reproducible Analysis Pipelines
content:
Journals and funders increasingly require data and code availability statements, but such statements rarely guarantee that the materials are usable. Our goal was to evaluate whether lightweight provenance capture reduces the effort needed to reproduce a published analysis. The model and data choices made in this study reflect a balance between realism and tractability, and each choice is justified in the sections that follow. This study was designed to address a gap that earlier reports left open, and the methods and data used here are described in enough detail to allow independent assessment. Replication, in which a new team repeats a study with new data, differs from reproduction, in which the original data and code are reused, and the two terms are often confused. Provenance records describe how a data product was derived, including the inputs, the software versions, the parameters and the sequence of transformation steps. Computational reproducibility means that an independent analyst can regenerate published results from the same code and data, yet many studies fall short of this standard.

A replication component repeated a subset of studies on new data to examine how sensitive the conclusions were to analytic choices. Model parameters were estimated by standard fitting routines, and convergence diagnostics were examined for every model that entered the results. Code provenance relied on version control history, with each result linked to the exact commit that produced it. A held-out portion of the data was reserved for validation and was not used for any tuning decision in the study. We sampled one hundred and twenty published analyses and attempted to rerun each using the archived code and data in a clean computing environment. Data provenance was recorded with persistent identifiers for each dataset, together with metadata describing its origin, licence and version. Provenance was captured with a workflow engine that logged inputs, outputs, parameters, container image digests and checksums of every file in the pipeline.

Reproducible epidemic forecasting code deserves particular attention because forecasts are produced under time pressure and are later used to judge a model. In our review of forecast hub submissions, we recorded for each weekly epidemic forecast the exact code commit, the container image, the version of the surveillance data and the random seed, and stored these with the submitted quantiles. Teams that archived this provenance could rerun a nowcast of incident cases or an Rt estimate months later and obtain the same ensemble inputs, whereas teams that overwrote their data snapshots could not. Pipelines for epidemic models should therefore capture data vintage as carefully as code, because reporting revisions change what the model saw. Workflow capture for forecasting pipelines costs little relative to the value of being able to audit a forecast after an outbreak has ended.

A limitation of the study is that some sources of uncertainty could not be quantified and are therefore described only qualitatively. Our estimates of reproducibility rates carry uncertainty from the sampling of projects, which were drawn from laboratories willing to participate. Numerical differences across hardware and library versions mean that bitwise reproduction is rarely achievable, and tolerance thresholds are a judgement. We report uncertainty intervals throughout and avoid presenting single numbers without a statement of their precision. Even a perfectly reproducible pipeline does not guarantee that the underlying result is correct, because reproduction repeats errors as faithfully as it repeats findings. The benefit of workflow tools may be overstated if early adopters are more careful researchers than average.

Machine-readable provenance supports automated checking and allows downstream users to assess whether a dataset is fit for their purpose. The main limitations of the study concern the data, the model assumptions, and the generalisability of the results to other settings. Training and incentives are as important as tools, since researchers respond to the requirements that reviewers and funders enforce. We recommend that repositories validate deposited code by rerunning it, and that journals reward reproducible workflows. A shared vocabulary for reproduction and replication would help to compare findings across disciplines. We recommend that future studies adopt similar reporting practice for their methods, data, and results so that findings can be compared.
